title: NavIC satellite NVS-03 reaches its working orbit, clearing the step where NVS-02 failed
dek: ISRO says four engine firings have lifted the satellite launched on October 30 into geosynchronous orbit and that it is in good health. In-orbit tests come next before NavIC can count it.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The navigation satellite NVS-03 has reached its intended geosynchronous orbit after four engine firings, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) said on Wednesday, November 4. That clears the step at which its predecessor, NVS-02, failed in 2025, and brings India's own satellite navigation system, NavIC, close to the minimum strength it needs to work on its own.

"Four orbit manoeuvres have been successfully completed with a cumulative LAM engine burn of 6164 seconds. With this the satellite has reached Geo Synchronous Orbit [35765 km x 36196 km] at an inclination of 29.980," ISRO said in its update, according to reports. The satellite is in good health, the agency said.

## Update: the orbit-raising

The GSLV-F18 rocket placed NVS-03 in a long oval orbit of 170.3 km by 38,080 km after lift-off at 11:51 pm IST on October 30, ISRO said on its mission page. The first firing of the satellite's own liquid apogee motor (LAM), lasting 2,174.8 seconds, was completed at 4:48 pm on October 31 and raised the low point of the orbit to about 5,478 km. Three more firings followed, taking the total burn time to 6,164 seconds, or nearly 103 minutes. ISRO's mission page says the satellite will be placed in the 111.75 degrees East orbital slot.

To avoid a repeat of the NVS-02 failure, ISRO flew NVS-03 with three pyro valves already open, ISRO Chairman V Narayanan said after the launch, according to reports. He said the decision was cleared after vibration and shock tests reviewed by a national committee chaired by former ISRO chief A S Kiran Kumar. On NVS-02, the signal that should have fired the oxidiser-line pyro valve never arrived, so its engine could not be started.

## The launch

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the navigation satellite NVS-03 on its GSLV-F18 rocket from Sriharikota at 11:51 pm IST on Friday, October 30, in a mission meant to bring India's own satellite navigation system, NavIC, back to the minimum strength it needs to work on its own.

The rocket lifted off from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, ISRO said in a post on X. One report said shortly after midnight that the rocket had injected the satellite of about 2,250 kg into its planned geosynchronous transfer orbit. The harder part of the mission now begins: in 2025 the previous satellite in the series, NVS-02, reached the same kind of orbit and then could not be moved any further.

## What happened

The GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, according to ISRO and reports. The rocket, about 50 metres tall and weighing about 420 tonnes at lift-off according to one report, uses a solid core booster with four liquid-fuelled strap-on motors, a liquid second stage and an Indian-built cryogenic upper stage that burns liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.

According to figures published in reports before the launch, the cryogenic stage was to release NVS-03 into a long oval orbit about 170 km above Earth at its lowest point and 37,023 km at its highest. From there the satellite must fire its own engine several times over the coming days to round off that orbit and climb to its working position about 36,000 km up, where it will appear to hang over the Indian region.

NVS-03 carries an Indian-built atomic clock alongside clocks bought from abroad, reports said. Accurate timekeeping is the heart of any satellite navigation system: receivers on the ground work out their position by measuring how long signals take to arrive from several satellites. The satellite also adds a civilian L1 signal, the band used by GPS and most consumer phones, to NavIC's existing L5 and S-band signals, which should make it easier for ordinary devices to use NavIC. The system is designed to cover India and an area up to about 1,500 km beyond its borders.

## Background

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), earlier called IRNSS, is India's regional alternative to the American GPS. It was built so that India would not have to depend on a foreign system for positioning and timing, which are used by everything from aircraft and ships to telecom networks, power grids and banking.

The system has been short of working satellites for some time. In a reply in Parliament on July 29, 2026, the government said only three satellites, IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I and NVS-01, were providing positioning, navigation and timing services, reports said. At least four are needed for a receiver to fix its position independently, and the full constellation is designed for seven.

The second-generation NVS series was meant to fix that. NVS-01 was launched in May 2023. NVS-02 followed in January 2025 on GSLV-F15, as ISRO's 100th launch from Sriharikota, and reached its transfer orbit. But the valves that should have let fuel and oxidiser flow to its main engine never opened, so the satellite could not be raised to its working orbit.

One report, citing the findings of ISRO's review, said that the fault was traced to a contact that had come loose in a connector on the oxidiser line. The valves involved are pyro valves, one-time switches opened by a small explosive charge, and the break cut off both the main and the backup signal at once. A failure analysis committee was headed by former ISRO chairman A S Kiran Kumar, according to another report.

Union Minister Jitendra Singh, who oversees the space department, has said the problems have been corrected and that the fix was tested on the communication satellite CMS-03, launched by an LVM3 rocket on November 2, 2025, one report said. Some reports before the launch said ISRO might open the pyro valves on the ground before lift-off this time, and Narayanan confirmed after the launch that it had done so.

## What they are saying

One report said before the launch that a successful deployment would restore NavIC's basic operational requirement of four satellites.

Space analyst Girish Linganna said in an interview that "the real test for NVS-03 begins where its sibling fell silent", a reference to the orbit-raising stage at which NVS-02 failed.

## What happens next

With the orbit-raising done, the satellite must now drift to its slot and go through in-orbit tests of its atomic clocks and navigation signals before it can be commissioned into service, a process that usually takes weeks. ISRO has not yet given a date for NVS-03 to start providing navigation.

Even then, NavIC will have only the bare minimum of four working navigation satellites. NVS-04 and NVS-05 are in their final stages of preparation, according to reports, and one more satellite will be needed after them to complete the planned seven.

## Key numbers

- Lift-off: 11:51 pm IST, October 30, 2026
- Rocket: GSLV-F18, the 20th GSLV flight
- Satellite mass: about 2,250 kg (one report gives 2,232 kg)
- Transfer orbit achieved: 170.3 km x 38,080 km (ISRO)
- Orbit-raising: four LAM firings, 6,164 seconds in total
- Final orbit: 35,765 km x 36,196 km, inclined at 29.98 degrees (ISRO, November 4)
- NavIC satellites providing navigation before this launch: 3 (government reply, July 2026)
- Minimum needed for independent positioning: 4; full design: 7
